data.title: No review, no commission: Claude is replacing Apple's App Store
data.description:
Author: Silicon Valley Alan Walker

This Tuesday, Claude added a button, and after seeing it, I felt: Apple's App Store has been collecting money for over a decade, and now someone is starting to circumvent it.

November 24th, this Tuesday, Anthropic added a button to the Claude desktop version called "Install as app," allowing users to install it as an application.

November 24th, this Tuesday, Anthropic added a button to the Claude desktop version called "Install as app," allowing users to install it as an application.

Many people didn't take it seriously. I did. This button does this: someone who's never written a single line of code tells Claude, "Make me an accounting tool," and a few minutes later, a real application appears on their Mac or Windows computer. It has an icon, can be opened independently, and will pop up notifications. If given enough permissions, it can even read, modify, and delete files on your computer. This application hasn't been reviewed by Apple, nor has it been stamped as "legitimate software," and Apple hasn't taken a single penny from it. I've been watching tech companies for thirty years, and I usually just glance at most feature updates and move on. This time, however, I read the official explanation twice from beginning to end, and one thought kept running through my mind: AI companies are starting to directly steal Apple's business. How big is the App Store? Apple itself has announced that from 2008 to 2022, developers earned over $320 billion on the App Store. In 2025, the App Store had an average of 850 million users per week, covering 175 countries and regions. Apple's total services revenue for fiscal year 2025 was $109.16 billion, with the App Store being the most crucial part. Claude is now eyeing this business: users spend nearly $150 billion annually on the App Store, and developers have accumulated hundreds of billions of dollars over the past decade. That day, I was sitting in Zombie Cafe on California Avenue in Palo Alto, looking at the official support page. When I saw the line "Can read, modify, or delete your files," I put my coffee down. To sum it up: Claude's move is aimed at Apple's App Store business, which is worth hundreds of billions of dollars annually and hundreds of billions of dollars cumulatively. 1. What's being launched this time is much more than just a new feature. It's the beginning of a complete app business. When Apple launched the App Store in 2008, it held five things in its hands: the tools for creating apps, the people creating apps, the way to get apps to you, the method of charging, and a set of rules that everyone had to follow. Of these five, Claude has released more than four this week, only lacking a public app store. 2. Who is it targeting? Apple's App Store. According to external estimates, Apple earns between 10-20 billion and nearly 30 billion US dollars annually from App Store commissions alone, with virtually no costs. Whoever can get users to install apps bypassing the App Store is cutting into Apple's profits. 3. Using Claude to develop apps has real advantages over downloading from the App Store: No programming skills required. No annual fees to Apple or need Apple's approval. No waiting in line for review. There's no 30% commission. The app is made by you alone; you can modify it as you please. 4. The money flows through a different channel; Apple can't reach you anymore. The App Store's revenue comes from every transaction. Claude's app doesn't have any transactions; users pay Claude's membership fee. 5. It's still in the testing phase, but the direction is clear. It only supports computers, not phones. It's labeled a beta version. Only five employees have been shown, and there's no public store. 6. The real battle is on mobile. The official documentation states that Linux, the web version, and mobile are not supported "at launch." This implies support will follow. Apple will truly be losing sleep when Claude's apps are finally available on mobile. I've done the math myself; in three to five years, Claude's system could potentially siphon billions to tens of billions of dollars annually from the App Store. How I calculated this will be explained in Section 6. How to use it: Three steps, one sentence to turn it into an application on your computer. First, let's talk about how to use it. If you can type and chat, you can use it. First, speak up. Open the Mac or Windows version of Claude and explain what you need in plain language. For example, "Batch rename photos by shooting date." Second, try it out, and keep revising if you're not satisfied. Claude will first create a small, usable program next to the chat window, officially called Artifact. Think of it as an application that hasn't been installed on your computer yet, placed next to the chat window for you to try out. Try it out, and if anything doesn't work, just tell it, and it will keep revising until you're satisfied. Third, click and install. Select "Install as app" from the menu and confirm. On your Mac, it will appear in the "Applications" folder, or you can drag it to the list of frequently used icons at the bottom of the screen. Visually, it looks exactly like the software you paid for. After installation, it can do the following: Use your Claude account directly; no need to apply for a separate password or key, and no additional payment. It deducts from your membership credit every time it uses Claude's features. It can use services you've already connected to in Claude, such as email, calendar, cloud storage, and documents. It can pop up notifications in the corner of the screen and display a small icon in the top menu bar. The official documentation specifically states that apps with menu bar icons continue running in the background even after the window is closed. It can automatically update. If you modify the original version in Claude, the installed version will update accordingly. It can be shared. You can send it to colleagues and friends, and they can install it too. Its accessibility to your computer is divided into three levels. The lowest level can only do what a webpage can do; it cannot access anything on your computer. The middle level offers features like pop-up alerts, keyboard shortcuts, keeping windows always on top, and tracking your mouse cursor's position. The highest level is called "Full Access." The official description states: "It can run any program, read, modify, or delete your files. It can do everything on your computer." This level is only for applications you've created; in the company version, applications created by colleagues can also be accessed. I put down my coffee because of this. Software that didn't exist a few minutes ago, without Apple's review or inspection, can access your folders and delete your documents simply by clicking "confirm." Apple's over-the-counter review system, built over a decade, is irrelevant to it. Ultimately, the only safeguard is whether you click "confirm." Here are a few more limitations. An internet connection and Claude login are required. It's currently a beta version, usable by both free and paid users. In the company and team editions, this feature is enabled by default, but "Full Access" is disabled by default; in the enterprise edition, the administrator must manually enable it. It doesn't work on mobile, web, or Linux for now. There's another crucial point: if the application developer stops sharing it or deletes the original, your installed version will stop working in about 20 minutes. How long someone shares something with you is up to them, not you. Think about what that means. A colleague made you a small expense reimbursement tool, which you used perfectly. Then, just before the end of the month when you needed to submit the form, he deleted the original version, and twenty minutes later, your app wouldn't open. With software bought on the App Store, even if the developer disappears, the one on your phone can at least continue to work for a while. Claude's apps are different; their fate is in the hands of the person who made them. This rule seems like a minor inconvenience now, but as the number of apps increases, whoever's app remains consistently online and usable will be recognized. Anthropic also showcased five apps made by their employees: a photo editing app with layer separation, a file manager, a tool to automatically organize folders, a tool for programmers to type commands in a black-and-white window, and a little gadget that displays computer status in the menu bar. If you check these five one by one, they are all Mac apps that people consistently pay for. I don't believe this is a coincidence. How profitable is the App Store? Apple runs a store, takes a cut of every sale, how much does it earn in a year? To understand what Claude is trying to grab, you need to understand Apple's calculations first. Apple releases information about how much developers earn every now and then. In mid-2017, developers collectively earned $70 billion on the App Store. By the end of 2022, it had reached $320 billion. In that final year alone, developers earned approximately $60 billion. Apple doesn't report its own share, but it can be deduced. For every digital product sold, Apple takes 15% to 30%, with the remainder going to the developer. Based on this ratio, CNBC estimates that users spent between $70 billion and $85 billion on the App Store in 2022. Appfigures estimates it will reach $91.3 billion in 2024. With a 15% to 30% commission, Apple's annual revenue from this alone would be between $10 billion and nearly $30 billion. For every $100 a user spends on the App Store, Apple pockets $15 to $30. And Apple spends almost nothing on this. The apps are written by the developers, and the developers pay for promotion themselves. Apple only provides the store, a set of review rules, and a system for collecting money. How significant is this business within Apple? In fiscal year 2025, Apple's services revenue reached $109.16 billion, exceeding $100 billion for the first time and becoming Apple's second-largest business after the iPhone. The App Store is the core of the services segment. There are over 2.3 billion Apple devices in use worldwide. Apple says that by 2025, the entire business driven by the App Store will be worth $1.4 trillion, of which $149 billion will be its share of digital goods and services. In simpler terms, the App Store is like a giant shopping mall. Apple doesn't sell goods itself; it rents out space to millions of developers, taking a 15% to 30% cut of every digital item sold. Who gets to open a store and what products are listed are entirely up to Apple. In 2022 alone, Apple rejected nearly 1.7 million app store listing applications. For example, if you spend 100 yuan in a mobile game, the game company gets 70, and Apple gets the remaining 30. They make the game, they attract the players, so why should Apple get that 30? Because they own the marketplace. This is what Claude is eyeing: hundreds of billions of dollars in digital consumption annually, plus the 10-20 billion to nearly 30 billion that Apple takes. What Anthropic wants to do: Follow Apple's path in 2008 and build its own app business. Apple built the App Store back then with five things. Looking at Claude's update one by one, it's clear what Anthropic wants to do. App development tools. Apple has a whole set of development tools. To make an iPhone app, you need to learn programming languages ​​and UI design, which takes at least six months. Claude's tool is Claude himself. All you need to do is speak. App developers. Apple relies on millions of professional programmers. Claude relies on everyone who uses Claude—accountants, teachers, salespeople, small shop owners—anyone can do it. The path to getting the app into the user's hands. Apple lets you search and download from the store. Claude offers "one-click installation" and "one-click sharing"—you create it, send it to a colleague, and they install it with a single click. The way to make money. Apple takes a cut from every transaction. Claude charges membership fees. The more apps are used, the easier it is to use up the monthly credit limit, and the more likely the user is to upgrade to a higher-priced tier. The rules governing order. Apple has review rules; apps that don't comply can't be listed. Claude uses the three levels of permissions mentioned earlier. Every time an app updates, you have to re-approve all previously granted permissions. If an app made by someone else requests the highest permissions, the system will issue a warning. Of the five, Claude already has more than four. What it lacks is a public app store. So what is Anthropic's goal? It sells AI usage; the more you use it, the more it earns. Every Claude app you install on your computer gives you another reason to use Claude every day. The official statement says that apps with menu bar icons continue running in the background even when the window is closed. Even when you're not looking at it, it's probably still working, connected to your email, calendar, and cloud storage. Users think they've installed a small software program. Actually, this small program is calling Claude for you every day, burning through your credit limit. A simple explanation: An app business is like a market: there need to be people selling goods, places to set up stalls, people collecting management fees, and people maintaining order. This week, Claude has distributed its "selling" capabilities to everyone; the delivery routes are open, and the rules are established. All that's missing is a public area where everyone can browse. It's not in a hurry to open it because most apps people are currently creating are for their own use and don't need yet. For example, you made a small tool for yourself to compile all the bills in your email every morning. It works great, so you share it with your company's finance department, and ten people install it and use it every day. This tool already has users; people help share it, and it's used daily. One day, Anthropic puts the shared apps into a public directory and gives the app developers a share of the profits, and a new app store just pops up. Why do I say it's still testing the waters? Look at how it chooses each step. It only focuses on computers because computer systems are less regulated, and nobody can stop it. Only beta versions are displayed, so they can be easily removed if anything goes wrong. Only the work of five employees is showcased as a preliminary example. The company version also has leeway: the team version is enabled by default, but the most alarming "full access" is disabled by default; the enterprise version is simply left to the administrator to decide whether to enable or disable, avoiding the security issues that large companies care about most. On the day the Apple App Store opened in July 2008, there were only about 500 apps. Who could have imagined then that more than a decade later it would distribute $320 billion to developers? What's better than the App Store: Five ways making your own app with Claude is better than downloading from the App Store

This section focuses on one thing: how making and installing apps with Claude is better than downloading from the App Store.

First, you don't need to know programming, just how to speak

Apps on the App Store are all written by professional programmers. Ordinary people have an idea, and they either wait for someone else to do it or pay someone to do it. With Claude, you just express your idea, and your app is ready in minutes. There are only so many people in the world who can write code, but everyone can speak.

Second, you don't need to pay Apple an annual fee, nor do you need Apple's "stamp." To sell software on Apple computers, developers first need to pay Apple $99 annually to register as Apple-recognized developers. Then, each software needs to go through two procedures, colloquially called "signing" and "notarization." Signing is like stamping the software with "who made this," allowing you to find the person responsible if something goes wrong. Notarization is like having Apple thoroughly check the software to ensure it's virus-free. Without these two steps, when a user double-clicks the software, the system will pop up a window saying "Unable to verify developer." Most people wouldn't dare install it after seeing these words. Windows has a similar warning. For apps made by Claude, none of these procedures are required. According to official statements, these apps borrow the identity of Claude's desktop version, which itself has already passed Apple and Microsoft's checks. The computer recognizes Claude, so there's no need to check each of Claude's smaller apps individually. Thirdly, there's no need to wait in line for approval; you can use it immediately after completion. Listing an app on the App Store requires submission to Apple for review, which can take anywhere from a day or two to several weeks, and if it's rejected, you have to revise and resubmit. In 2022, Apple rejected nearly 1.7 million app store listing applications. Claude, on the other hand, officially states in black and white: "Anthropic will not review these apps before you install them." Done? Click, install. You have an idea today, you can use it today, no need to wait for approval. Fourth, there's no 30% commission. On the App Store, Apple takes 15% of every app purchase and every in-app purchase, up to a 30% cut. Claude's app doesn't involve any buying or selling; you're paying the standard membership fee. Developers don't share revenue with Apple, and users don't have to pay extra for Apple's commission. Fifth, it's tailor-made for you, can be modified at any time, and can use your own data. Software on the App Store is designed for millions of users; its functions are fixed, and if it doesn't fit your needs, you have to make do. Claude's app is made just for you. You can say, "Move this button to the right, and add an export function," and it will change within minutes. It can also directly read your connected email, calendar, and cloud storage, gathering your own data for use. Most software on the App Store can't do this.

Simple Explanation

The App Store is like a clothing store, full of ready-made clothes, with only a few sizes. You have to queue to get in, and the store takes a cut at checkout. Claude is like having a tailor come to your house. He makes what you want on the spot, alters it if it doesn't fit, and uses your own fabric.

For example

You want a menu widget that reminds you to drink water every morning and also tracks how many glasses you drank this week.

Previously, you had to search the App Store, compare them one by one, download them, and check if they charged a subscription fee. Now, just tell Claude, and it's on your computer in minutes. From start to finish, no developers were paid, and it didn't go through Apple's review process. The technology to "install" web pages as applications on a computer has existed for a long time. Google promoted it in 2015, and Apple planned to allow Safari to save web pages as applications in 2023, but almost no one used it. The reason is simple: the technology has always been there; what was lacking were people to develop applications. Claude has transformed the application development community from a small group of programmers to everyone. Looking at these five points together, Claude completely bypassed the usual barriers Apple uses to make money: entry requirements, procedures, reviews, and commission. Apple claims these barriers are to protect users. But for someone who just wants a simple reminder to drink water, none of these barriers apply. How much can Claude take: Let's do the math, how much money can Claude take from Apple? In this section, I'll do the math. A disclaimer: the numbers below are my own estimates based on publicly available data; these are my own calculations, not predictions from any organization. First, let's see how big the pie is. Apple says that digital goods and services spending on the App Store will reach $149 billion in 2025. This is the money users spend on apps, games, subscriptions, and in-app purchases, from which Apple primarily takes a cut. Now let's see which areas Claude can penetrate. Games, videos, and music are the major areas he can't easily penetrate in the short term. The easiest areas to penetrate are utility and productivity apps: budgeting, note-taking, scheduling, document organization, photo editing, and various small assistants. These apps are not complex and can be created with just a single line of code, and many charge a monthly subscription fee. Looking at a three- to five-year timeframe, we can consider two scenarios. To be conservative, Claude takes a 5% cut of digital spending from the App Store, primarily from utility apps. That's about $7.5 billion out of $149 billion. $7.5 billion that would normally be spent on the App Store is instead going into Claude's membership fees. Apple loses roughly $1.1 billion to $2.2 billion annually in commission. To take a more radical view, Claude's apps, once on mobile, replaced utility, productivity, learning, and some entertainment apps, taking away 20% of the market share. That's roughly $30 billion in annual consumer spending moving elsewhere, and Apple losing $4.5 billion to $9 billion annually. How much is that worth to Anthropic? Not every single one of those $7.5 billion to $30 billion will go into Anthropic's pocket. Users create their own tools, saving some money. But if a significant portion of that goes towards membership fees for users upgrading to the next tier, it becomes a huge business. Even assuming the entire sum is converted, and using a price-to-sales ratio (P/S ratio) of 10 to 20, typical for established platform companies, this corresponds to a value of $75 billion to $600 billion. The P/S ratio is how many times a company's market capitalization is relative to its annual revenue. This doesn't even include the biggest part. Apple says the App Store drives a $1.4 trillion business, the bulk of which comes from users buying physical goods, ordering takeout, and booking hotels within apps. Apple doesn't take a cut of these transactions, but each order requires you to open an app first. If people become increasingly accustomed to simply telling Claude, "Book me a hotel," without even bothering to open the app, then whoever takes that line will be at the forefront of this $1.4 trillion business. That position is worth far more than a cut. Apple makes money by collecting "tolls," taking a cut for every transaction. Since Claude's apps don't involve transactions, Apple doesn't collect its commission. A portion of the money users previously spent on App Store apps goes into Claude's membership fees, thus eliminating Apple's cut. For example, a budgeting app might charge $30 annually on the App Store, with Apple taking $4.50 to $9. Now, if you have Claude create one that reads your inbox, automatically categorizes your bills, and alerts you at the end of the month about any overspending, you don't have to pay the $30. The developer doesn't receive their commission, and Apple doesn't take a penny from the app. The extra cost you make is a small portion of your Claude membership credit. Tonight, you can do one thing. Open your credit card statement and count the apps that automatically deduct money from your account every month. How many of them could you have done by simply talking to Claude? This is Apple's biggest headache. Their commission model has a prerequisite: there must be transactions. If an app is only used by you and there are no transactions from beginning to end, Apple can't find a single transaction to take a cut from. This kind of impact has already happened once this year. On January 30th, Anthropic released 11 plugins for Claude's office assistant, Cowork, covering legal, sales, finance, and marketing. According to DeepLearning.AI, in the four days following the plugin releases, the market capitalization of software companies in the S&P Software & Services Index evaporated by over $285 billion. Wall Street called this the "SaaS apocalypse." SaaS refers to enterprise software that charges monthly or annually. Last time, the companies that sold enterprise software were the targets. This time, Claude targeted the software store itself. Who will be impacted first: Those whose livelihoods will be taken away first are paid productivity tools for computers, independent developers, and programmers. If Claude's path succeeds, three groups will be the first to suffer. The first group will be paid productivity tools for Macs: Hazel for automatic file organization, iStat Menus for monitoring computer performance in the menu bar, Warp for programmers to type commands, and Pixelmator for layered image editing. Almost every one of the five employee projects Anthropic showcased corresponds to a paid software that has been selling for many years. The second wave consists of independent developers. These are people who work alone, making software. Some make tens of thousands of dollars a year selling a small tool, supporting themselves. Previously, their competitors were other developers, comparing features, prices, and ratings. Going forward, their competitors will be their own users. Users won't search for "bulk name change tool" anymore; they'll directly tell Claude, "Change my name." The paying users he's built up over the years may gradually become obsolete. The most painful thing going forward is that he won't even know who he's competing against. Before, if someone copied his software, he could see it, lower the price, add features, and explain in the comments. Now, users will quietly make their own, won't give him a bad review, and won't say goodbye; they'll just not renew their subscription next month. He only saw the subscription curve in the backend gradually declining, but couldn't find the reason. The company's IT department was also in this wave. Previously, if the finance department wanted a small internal system, they had to submit a request to IT and wait in line for three months. Now, the finance department staff can do it themselves. This feature is enabled by default in the team version, and the enterprise version administrator can enable it with a simple click. The third wave: Programmers. Imagine an engineer who has been writing web page code for fifteen years at a large company. This Tuesday afternoon, he curiously clicked on Claude and created a small tool in ten minutes, almost identical to the requirement he had waited two weeks for last month. He closed his laptop and sat in the parking lot for a long time. Currently, Claude is still only making small tools. But you have to understand, today's Claude is the worst it's ever been. Independent evaluation agency METR has measured that the length of tasks AI can independently complete roughly doubles every 7 months. At this rate, it will double five to eight times in three to five years, reaching 32 to 256 times its current size. Today it might be making a small photo editing app; by then, it might be making professional-grade design software. At that point, the impact will extend far beyond just a few small Mac gadgets. Professional software that charges hundreds of dollars a year for subscriptions—for designers, video editors, and project managers—will have to rethink why users should continue to pay them annually. Before the invention of printing, copying books was a respectable craft. Later, copyists became unemployed, regardless of their handwriting quality; the act of "copying" itself no longer required human intervention. Today, many programmers translate human needs into code that computers can execute. Once AI can directly understand human speech, this intermediate step will become less human-intensive. For example, a photographer wants a tool to batch rename photos by shooting date and location, and then organize them into folders by city. Five years ago, he had to find pre-written programs on forums or pay someone to write one. Today, he can just ask Claude. In another five years, he might not even need to ask: Claude, seeing him manually renaming photos after exporting, will proactively ask him, "Do you want me to make you a tool?" The first software to be replaced is always the "simple and useful" kind. Unfortunately, most software in the world is like that. Next step: Right now it's just for computers. Apple will really have a headache when Claude's apps can be installed on the iPhone. There's a sentence in the official description that I read several times: "At launch," Linux, web version, and mobile are not yet supported. The phrase "at launch" is specifically added because they plan to support them later. Computers are just the first step; mobile phones are the real territory. Apple's $109.16 billion in service revenue and 850 million weekly App Store users are mostly from iPhones. Claude started with computers because Mac and Windows are less restrictive. Software that has already passed review can open new windows and read/write files within itself, which is allowed by the rules. The iPhone is much stricter. Apple's review rules, section 4.7, allow a large application to contain smaller applications built using web technologies. However, there are two conditions: First, without Apple's approval, the large application cannot expose the core functions of the phone to these smaller applications. Second, the large application must submit a directory clearly listing all the smaller applications within it. This is where the trouble lies. Claude's applications are made by each individual for themselves; a thousand people, a thousand different designs, and they change daily. This catalog is simply impossible to submit. This rule governs a large application containing dozens or hundreds of smaller applications, each with a fixed name and function, which can be listed. But Claude's applications are created by users with a single sentence; there's no limit to their number, and their appearance changes daily. This kind of thing is very difficult to fit into a list. Apple allows you to open a "store within a store" within its marketplace, but you have to submit a list to Apple first of what each store sells. For example, you created a water reminder for yourself, and your colleague created an expense reimbursement assistant. Each of these apps has only one user worldwide, and they might change tomorrow. How would you submit this list? Apple has already taken action. In November 2025, Apple launched the "Mini Program Partner Program": for purchases made through mini programs within large apps that meet certain conditions, the commission rate was reduced from 30% to 15%. The idea is clear: don't block them, take a smaller commission, and continue making money. But this tactic didn't work on Claude. Claude's app doesn't have any transactions, so the reduced commission rate is irrelevant. Looking ahead, I predict the likely sequence will be: 1. More and more apps will emerge. Users first create tools for themselves on their computers, then share them with colleagues and friends. Useful tools quickly spread within the company and social circles. 2. A public directory emerges. With so many shared applications, there needs to be a place where they can be found. Anthropic simply puts the publicly shared applications into a directory, sorted by usage, and the "Claude App Store" is created. 3. Revenue sharing with app developers. When someone uses your app and calls Claude, they use their own credit limit. Anthropic takes a share of that and shares it with the developers, making app development a profitable business. In 2008, Apple attracted millions of developers by offering a 70% cut to developers and a 30% cut to Apple. 4. Entering the mobile market. Users are used to having an app available simply by speaking on a computer, and sooner or later they will ask: Why can't it be the same on a mobile phone? At that point, Apple will face two difficult paths. If they release Claude's app on the iPhone, they will lose their App Store commission. If they don't, users will feel that Apple is preventing them from using good content. Either way, Apple will have to give up a portion of the money it has been steadily collecting for over a decade. For the past decade or so, all companies have been desperately trying to squeeze into those few slots on your phone's home screen. From now on, which apps you have on your phone won't matter as much. Whether you want to book a hotel, keep track of your expenses, or organize photos, the money will flow to whoever's first message you send. Previously, you could only do what the software had. Starting this Tuesday, the software will look exactly what you want.

data.title: Post-Trump Era: The End of Regulatory Arbitrage, the Resurgence of Decentralized Narratives

Author: Gu Yu, ChainCatcher

In recent weeks, the crypto market has continued its downward trend, with BTC prices hitting a near two-year low. The main reason for this decline is not internal industry developments or regulatory aspects, but rather the resonance of the external macroeconomic environment: a strong US dollar, hawkish interest rate expectations, the waning of the tech stock rebound, and risk aversion driven by escalating tensions in the Middle East.

Looking at a longer timeframe, we can see that the rise and fall of the crypto market has become increasingly closely related to political dynamics in recent years, especially with the Trump administration in the United States.

Since Trump took office in early 2025, the industry has faced a clearly friendly administration for the first time: the SEC withdrew its case, pro-crypto officials took office, the GENIUS Act became law, and the strategic Bitcoin reserve entered the agenda.

Every factor was quickly priced into the market, making policy the most sensitive switch for market movements. On November 4th, this switch was flipped to the other side. The "blue wave" of the US midterm elections concluded, and on the same day, the Democrats won control of both the House and Senate, and will take over the new Congress in January 2027. Trump-related assets such as WLFI and Trumppp plummeted by 10-20%, with year-to-date declines exceeding 75%. For the past two years, distance from the White House was a factor in valuation; now, it has become a risk factor requiring a discount. This is not a typical adjustment of politically sensitive assets, but a concentrated revaluation of the political premium in the crypto industry. Now, the crypto industry needs to prepare for the post-Trump era. Attributing all changes solely to a Democratic victory underestimates the industry's own problems. In fact, cracks had already appeared before the midterm elections. On September 15th, the US Senate failed to advance the procedural vote on the CLARITY Act by a vote of 49 to 50, far short of the required 60 votes. Triple Point Strategy, in its November 17th recap, pointed out that the core obstacle to the bill was not simply the characterization of tokens, but the ethical controversy surrounding the crypto interests of public officials and their families. This means that even with Republicans still controlling Congress, the crypto industry has failed to translate its political advantage into market structure legislation. The midterm elections merely amplified existing contradictions, rather than creating them. More problematic is that Trump is both the industry's most important political driving force and a source of conflicting interests. A Reuters survey on October 27 estimated that the Trump family would earn approximately $2.3 billion from crypto businesses between mid-2024 and April 2026. Trump has consistently denied any conflict between his business interests and his presidential duties, but this has not eliminated political resistance. "Many key figures in the crypto space have deeply tied themselves to the Trump family, and these costs are now likely to materialize," Austin Campbell, an adjunct professor at NYU's Stern School of Business and a former banker, told Bloomberg. Essentially, when regulatory friendliness coincides with benefits for the president's family, crypto policy becomes difficult for opponents to perceive as neutral technology policy. Trump helped the industry open doors in Washington, but also saddled the entire industry with an expensive partisan label. Bipartisan approaches cannot simply be about sharing money with one side. The industry was not unprepared. Reuters' pre-election statistics showed that by late October, crypto-related groups had spent approximately $176 million in the midterm elections, covering more than 100 campaigns, attempting to build a congressional coalition that could transcend Trump's term. Colin McLaren, director of government relations at the Solana Policy Institute, called the spending “an investment for the future,” aiming to ensure the industry has clear regulations “for the next 100 years.” Looking at the partial results, the money wasn’t entirely ineffective. According to Triple Point Strategy, as of November 17, candidates supported by the Fairshake network won 33 out of 36 November runoff elections. However, in the crucial Ohio Senate race, over $60 million in crypto-related spending failed to prevent Sherrod Brown, a longtime critic of the industry, from returning to the Senate. This contrast is closer to reality than either an “industry crushing defeat” or an “industry landslide victory”: political money can still influence some elections, but it cannot automatically buy legislative consensus. More alarmingly, Reuters found that many ads run by crypto political action committees barely touched on crypto, focusing instead on issues like taxes and immigration. This suggests the industry is more focused on building political deterrence than on gaining clear public authorization for digital assets. Following the election, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse stated, "The new Congress, the same mission: to establish clear rules in America." Crypto Innovation Council CEO Ji Kim also emphasized, "Digital assets have always been a bipartisan issue, and we are ready to work with both new and established members of Congress." However, a truly bipartisan approach cannot simply hand out checks to both sides. If the industry calls for departisanship while rejecting conflict-of-interest constraints, consumer protection, and clearer regulatory accountability, then this is not depoliticization, but merely turning a single political dependency into a long-term lobbying cost. Compliance has shifted from a benefit to a hurdle. A change in political winds does not mean that the institutional achievements of the past two years will be wiped out overnight. The GENIUS Act has become federal law, and repealing it requires new legislation. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued final rules for implementing the act on October 21, covering reserve assets, redemption, risk management, auditing, and capital requirements, and will take effect on January 18, 2027. While legislation is stalled, administrative oversight continues. Two days after the CLARITY Act was blocked, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) introduced a temporary "innovation exemption" for tokenized stock trading on September 17. In a statement, SEC Chairman Paul Atkins acknowledged that this measure is merely a transitional arrangement and "must ultimately be sustained by lasting rules." Therefore, the regulatory landscape over the next two years is unlikely to be a complete regression, but rather a slowdown in congressional legislation and continued development of executive rules, whose long-term effectiveness will still be constrained by the courts and the next administration. For businesses, this brings a more realistic change: compliance is no longer just a scarce story used to boost valuations, but a fundamental cost that continuously consumes capital, human resources, and management effort. Large institutions can share these costs, while small and medium-sized teams may be excluded by licensing, auditing, and legal expenses. Regulatory certainty is a public good, but compliance capabilities may become a private moat. The industry once hoped that regulation would eliminate uncertainty; now it must answer: are clear rules promoting competition or helping a few large institutions "get on board and close down"? "I think the era of lax regulation is almost over. At most, there will be another CLARITY bill next year. Regulatory arbitrage will come to an end, and the next wave of market activity will return to the original narrative. Considering the current bottom of the cycle, the next wave of decentralization may be coming (perhaps in 2028)," said crypto KOL Chen Mo. With the weakening of political dividends, the market focus may return to the decentralized narrative, with stablecoin payments and asset tokenization being highly anticipated. However, these two main themes also need to be weeded out of the narrative bubble. Visa Onchain Analytics data shows that adjusted stablecoin trading volume reached $1.79 trillion in June 2026, a year-on-year increase of 125%. This figure filters out some bot transfers, exchange fund transfers, and duplicate smart contract transactions, indicating that on-chain USD settlement is indeed expanding. However, "adjusted trading volume" still includes DeFi, liquidity management, and other activities, and cannot all be considered as physical payments. It demonstrates the resilience of stablecoins as settlement infrastructure, but it has not yet proven that the mass payment revolution is complete. Tokenized stocks show a similar contrast. Data from RWA.xyz in early November showed that the related asset size was approximately $3.9 billion; however, as OKXICE prepared to launch on November 23, Bloomberg statistics showed that 67 companies had already opposed its plan. Of the initial 62 companies targeted, 56 objected, and the six that did not publicly object were all affiliated with the crypto industry. "Many stock issuers are not focusing on tokenized stocks," said Ian De Bode, acting CEO of Ondo Finance. "The existing system works well for them." This is more concerning than the growth in the size of tokenized assets: the crypto industry can quickly build trading platforms, but it may not be able to persuade issuers, institutions, and users to migrate just as quickly. Regulation provides access, not demand; licenses provide qualifications, not moats. Infrastructure can be built first, but issuers may not follow. The crypto industry has been good at moving financial products on-chain in the past, but has rarely demonstrated that these products are cheaper, more transparent, or easier to use on-chain than on the original system. If technological innovation can only provide new trading venues but not new trust structures, the "native narrative" remains merely packaging. In conclusion, over the past few years, Trump has both helped the crypto industry open the doors to Washington and burdened it with a more difficult-to-remove label of conflict of interest, potentially becoming a "liability" for the industry. Labels are easy to attach but hard to remove—they don't disappear automatically with an election, nor are they automatically cleared by a change of president. Political advantages can inflate valuations, but they cannot replace real demand. A receding premium is not a bad thing; it simply returns the valuation to the business. The post-Trump era won't be defined by who enters the White House in 2028, but by a more direct question: what will the crypto industry have left when Washington stops providing additional premiums? Neither the ruling nor opposition governments can drive product innovation for the industry, and "returning to innovation" cannot be an excuse to revert to unlimited token issuance, regulatory arbitrage, and subsidy-driven growth. The political retreat is not the end, but a forced return—a return to more fundamental questions: can the system protect users? Can products create value? Does the demand truly exist? Only when these questions are answered can the industry truly overcome this downturn.

data.title: Bear Market Reflections: The Bitcoin Narrative Has Never Failed; Patient Holding Is Worth It
data.description:
Author: Jeff Park, Partner at ParaFi Capital; Translated by Shaw, Jinse Finance

Looking back over the past few weeks, I have to admit that this Bitcoin cycle has been the most psychologically difficult I've ever experienced. And I've personally experienced all bull and bear cycles (painfully).

Currently, all assets are experiencing a synchronized decline at the multi-sigma level. If Bitcoin could break free and move independently, this should have been a historically significant observation window.

In fact, many of the core narratives supporting Bitcoin should be playing out right now: The current global situation is turbulent, institutional trust is at an all-time low, and ambitions for surveillance and control are at their peak; in addition, there are real cryptographic risks that could disrupt our existing world order. Theoretically, Bitcoin offers a completely different path—though it's not perfect in reality. Looking back over the past fifteen years, I'm not even sure if a more favorable environment could emerge in the future to make people realize the value of Bitcoin. However, the reality is that Bitcoin hasn't broken out of this independent hedging trend; meanwhile, other assets seem "more attractive." The temptation to switch positions and find opportunities with better capital costs is incredibly strong. As an investor, I understand this deeply. Perhaps for the first time, I'm finding it difficult to figure out which catalyst I should be waiting for. <**Federal Reserve Policy?** I can find many other assets with equally high upside potential, but with much lower basis risk. <**Sovereign Nations Adopting Bitcoin?** The White House seems more interested in acquiring equity in American companies right now. <**Continuous Institutional Entry After ETF Launch?** If the three-year annualized return is only 9%, but the actual volatility is as high as 40%, this logic doesn't hold water. In the past, exchange or project failures could be absorbed because we knew these were just superficial problems; as long as the asset itself wasn't ineffective, it would eventually be repaired. But what if people start to believe that Bitcoin itself has become ineffective? Frankly speaking, an asset only truly fails when it can no longer deliver on its initial promises. We need to constantly remind ourselves: Bitcoin's promises haven't collapsed. The truth is, it never promised a target price, a correlation, or a catalyst for price increases as we might expect. What it truly promises is a fallback: no increase in total supply, no auditable settlements, and no stripping of ownership. In a world where more and more things are merely "granted the right to use" rather than "owned," you can still hold this asset without anyone's permission. This fallback remains intact to this day. A safety net doesn't lose value just because no one uses it temporarily; its value lies precisely in the fact that it remains even when all other channels are locked. So, if anything is "failing" now, perhaps it's just our patience. This is probably the price to pay for having a safety net in advance. This answer isn't comforting, but it's true. Therefore, we might need to prepare for hedging: the world will become more insane than we imagine. Previously unimaginable tail risks may materialize one by one. Imagine a severe cyber crisis, where the underlying structure of the open internet is rewritten in ways we can't predict; imagine an extreme risk: governments constantly infringe on privacy, freedom of speech, and other rights, forcing people to live "offline"; imagine a world where taxes continuously plunder wealth, automation relentlessly exploits labor, and surveillance systems completely erode privacy. I'm not sure I want to live in such a world, nor do I know what kind of financial system will emerge. But we seem to be gradually moving towards this grim situation. In my view, Bitcoin's most fundamental value ultimately boils down to one thing: it proves that a fallback option still exists. And the essence of an escape route is a narrow exit—once everyone realizes its value, it can no longer accommodate everyone. Therefore, I believe it's worthwhile to continue holding this call option. Often, the logic is that simple.

data.title: Will Strategy be liquidated?
data.description:
Strategy's 850,000 Bitcoins have resulted in a paper loss of $14 billion, as institutions have calculated their liquidation price.

Strategy's announcement on November 23rd clearly states:

The company currently holds a total of 851,305 Bitcoins, with an average cost of $75,446. Bitcoin is currently around $60,000, which is 20% lower than their cost.

The company holds 850,000 Bitcoins, representing 4.2% of the total Bitcoin supply. The answer calculated by institutions might surprise you: there was no liquidation price. Strategy's September quarterly report stated that none of these 850,000 Bitcoins were collateralized. The money they borrowed was primarily in convertible bonds, not loans secured by Bitcoin, so there was no possibility of forced liquidation at a certain price. Will he be able to hold on? Let's add up all the money he needs to repay: $6.7 billion in convertible bond principal and $14.1 billion in preferred stock, totaling $20.8 billion. Dividing $20.8 billion by 850,000 Bitcoins, Bitcoin would need to drop to $24,460 for him to just barely have enough to repay. If we also include his $4.8 billion in cash, this line would be even lower, around $18,800. It's about to fall another 60% from the current price. But this doesn't mean Saylor is without pressure. What really needs attention is another piece of data: He pays approximately $1.51 billion annually in preferred stock dividends and convertible bond interest. The largest portion of this is from STRC preferred stock, with an annual interest rate of 12%. Where does the money come from? Strategy has set aside a dollar reserve specifically for these payments. It currently has $3.73 billion, enough to cover approximately 30 months of payments. Last week, it removed $1 billion from this reserve for other purposes. The quarterly report also outlines two methods for replenishing reserves when they become insufficient: issuing new shares or selling Bitcoin. It has already sold some this year. From May to August, Strategy sold 6,948 Bitcoins, receiving $432 million, which was used to pay dividends and repurchase preferred stock. Aside from the 32 coins sold at the end of May, the remaining 6,916 coins were all sold below cost. The cheapest sale averaged $59,256, which is the current price. However, he's started buying again now, having bought 457 coins last week. But the money comes from issuing new common stock. When the stock price is good, he can issue shares; when the stock price is bad and he can't issue more, he can only use Bitcoin. Therefore, Saylor won't be liquidated. But he's a big spender who needs cash flow. He already sold once when the price was around 60,000 and the stock price was weakening. Do you think Saylor will sell again this time?

data.title: Trump angrily denounces GDP data as "wrong," implying it influenced the midterm elections.
data.description:
Author: Xiao Yanyan, Jinshi Data

US President Trump on Thursday accused US economic data of a "record error" and demanded an immediate investigation. Previously, data released by the US Department of Commerce showed that the annualized growth rate of real GDP in the third quarter was significantly revised upward from the initial estimate of 3.4% to 4.3%, indicating that the US economy performed significantly better than previously expected.

Trump posted on the Truth Social platform, **hinting that the initially released economic data may have influenced the outcome of the 2026 midterm elections.** In this election, the Democratic Party won control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives and won several governorships.

... Trump wrote: “I want to wish everyone a Happy Thanksgiving, even those who released false economic data shortly before the election and only corrected it yesterday. I wish them a Happy Thanksgiving. The corrected data shows that the actual GDP growth rate was 4.3%, not 3.4%. This is a record error, and so serious that it should be investigated immediately.” Without providing any evidence, Trump claimed: “The truth has just been revealed: the real economic data released before the election was fake.” He added in the post: “I demand an immediate investigation into this. This is not a small mistake, but a very serious, deliberate mistake.” However, historical data does not support Trump’s claim of a “record error.” This 0.9 percentage point upward revision of GDP growth is the largest since the second quarter of 2020. At the time, the US GDP growth rate was revised upward by 1.2 percentage points. Looking at all revisions from initial estimates to the second published data since 1990, this upward revision ranks 16th largest, with four other quarters seeing revisions of 0.9 percentage points. Despite this, the adjustment is still significantly higher than the usual range. The average revision between the initial estimate and the second published data for US GDP is about 0.43 percentage points, making this revision approximately twice that average. White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC that the upward revision shows Trump's policies are "working out" and the US economy is performing better than expected. GDP data revisions are not uncommon, and strong growth is putting pressure on the Federal Reserve. Revisions to US economic data are not new. The initial GDP data typically relies on partial survey results and preliminary estimates. As more survey feedback is collected, the Department of Commerce updates the data, so discrepancies between subsequent figures and initial estimates are common. US GDP data undergoes multiple revisions over the next five years. After the final revision, the average absolute error between the second published data and the final data is 1.14 percentage points. The preliminary estimate for third-quarter GDP was released in early November, just days before the midterm elections. The data at that time was already better than economists' expectations and showed that US economic growth had accelerated significantly compared to the second quarter. Therefore, some on Wall Street believe that this upward revision simply further confirms the trend of continued US economic growth. Jim Baird, chief investment officer of Plante Moran Financial Advisors, stated that this upward revision further highlights the contradiction between US economic performance and monetary policy: economic growth is quite strong, but this resilience also gives the Federal Reserve more reason to continue raising interest rates. He said, "The U.S. economy is not just barely maintaining growth, but continues to demonstrate considerable resilience. Consumers are still spending, businesses are still investing, and there are few signs that restrictive monetary policy is creating significant cracks in the overall economic expansion." Strong economic data is reinforcing market expectations that the Federal Reserve will continue to tighten monetary policy. According to the CME FedWatch tool, traders currently expect a near 100% probability of a rate hike by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its December meeting, and anticipate a further rate hike in January. This means that the upward revision of GDP has not only triggered Trump's questioning of the data revision process, but has also made the market further focus on the impact of economic resilience on the Fed's interest rate decisions.

Over the past year, listed mining companies have adopted almost identical strategies to cope with the bear market: selling off their Bitcoin holdings while transferring electricity and facilities to AI companies. The consensus in the market was that mining companies were withdrawing en masse and turning to AI, which was more profitable.

However, in November, the AI ​​sector also experienced significant volatility. In the two weeks following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation and subsequent reinstatement, the stock prices of mining companies that transitioned to AI also fluctuated wildly. This means that the AI ​​business that mining companies originally used to hedge against cryptocurrency prices is becoming a new source of risk.

I. Mining rigs are still running, but mining is no longer profitable

According to Hashrate Index data, as of November 25th, the Bitcoin hashrate price fell to $27.74 per PH per day, a near one-year low. However, the 7-day average hashrate of the entire network is still 1048.8 EH/s, and there has been no large-scale shutdown of mining rigs. Hashrate Index predicts that the difficulty adjustment on November 27th will increase by approximately 8.6%.

Regarding miner revenue, according to Newhedge data, total miner revenue in October was approximately $1.215 billion, the highest in 11 months; entering November, revenue so far is only about $740 million, and at this rate, total revenue for the month will be significantly lower than October's.

The cost pressure on listed mining companies has already become apparent. CoinShares' Q2 mining report shows that the weighted average cash cost for listed mining companies to mine one Bitcoin was approximately $75,500, while the Bitcoin price at the end of the quarter was only $58,400, causing the industry as a whole to fall below the cash break-even point.

The price of Bitcoin has now returned to this level. Twenty One Capital CEO Rapha Zagury previously stated that Bitcoin is experiencing its first-ever hashrate bear market, with fewer and fewer listed mining companies able to continue large-scale mining. II. Who is selling Bitcoin? Mining is not profitable, so mining companies are starting to sell their coins. According to Lookonchain statistics, as of November 10th, 14 listed companies have sold a total of 108,247 Bitcoins this year, worth approximately $8.08 billion, the vast majority of which were sold by mining companies. MARA and Riot sold 40,581 and 20,264 Bitcoins respectively, accounting for more than half of the total. Glassnode also points out that while listed mining companies have held onto their mined Bitcoins for years, and even bought some additional ones, they have sold nearly half of their reserves since January of this year. These Bitcoins are now being used to fund the transformation of AI data centers. Their charts show a net decrease of approximately 27,000 Bitcoins in November alone, the largest drop on record. On another note, even when selling Bitcoins, the purposes differ from company to company. MARA disclosed in its Q3 shareholder letter that it sold 13,597 Bitcoins at an average price of approximately $81,039 at the end of the quarter, raising approximately $1.1 billion, of which $750 million was used to pay off Bitcoin mortgage loans. Previously, MARA had sold cryptocurrency to repurchase approximately $1 billion in convertible bonds, reducing its debt by $1.4 billion in the first three quarters, a 37% decrease. This means MARA's cryptocurrency sales were primarily to repay the leverage left over from its previous expansion. Riot, on the other hand, invested the proceeds from its cryptocurrency sales in data centers. According to its Q3 financial report, Riot sold 20,264 Bitcoins in the first three quarters of this year, raising approximately $1.5 billion, mainly for data center construction. It did not conduct any equity financing throughout the year. III. Betting on AI: Where Did the Money from Cryptocurrency Sales Go? Mining companies' bets on AI have a very direct calculation behind them. CoinShares estimates that each megawatt of AI computing power can bring in approximately $1.5 million in profit annually, while Bitcoin mining only generates about $500,000. The capital market is also willing to pay a premium for this. Benoît Pellevoizin, Managing Director of CoinShares France, stated that mining companies that have signed contracts for AI capacity are trading at an average of 12.9 times their forward sales, while those without contracts are only trading at 3.7 times. The transformation narrative reached its peak in September when Grayscale renamed its Bitcoin Mining ETF to the AI ​​Hashrate ETF, changing its ticker symbol from MNRS to GCPU, and switching its tracking index to the Indxx High Performance Computing Index. However, the other side of this equation is the enormous investment required. CoinShares estimates that converting a mining farm into AI infrastructure costs between $8 million and $15 million per megawatt, more than ten times the cost of building a mining farm. According to BlocksBridge Consulting, the capital expenditures of nine listed mining companies reached $5.11 billion in the first half of this year, while AI and high-performance computing revenue was only $341 million during the same period, meaning the investment was 15 times the revenue. From a transformation perspective, mining companies can be broadly categorized into three types. The first type consists of landlords with long-term leases, represented by Riot, TeraWulf, and Cipher. Riot leased its entire Corsicana campus for 15 years, a contract valued at approximately $28 billion, with its 10-Q filing showing Anthropic as the tenant. TeraWulf signed a 20-year lease with Anthropic, worth approximately $19 billion. It's also worth noting that most of these leases won't commence until the second half of 2027, and the long-term revenue of several mining companies is tied to the same AI company. The second type comprises self-operated computing power providers, represented by IREN. IREN procures its own GPUs and provides computing power services to clients like Microsoft, offering greater revenue flexibility but also bearing the risks of GPU depreciation and customer concentration. The third category consists of mining companies whose transformation has not yet been implemented, a typical example being MARA. It sold the most cryptocurrencies this year, but its shareholder letter shows that it has not signed a single data center lease to date, and the only signed AI contract is a four-year, $79 million GPU service contract with its subsidiary Exaion. In November, when AI stocks experienced increased volatility, MARA reiterated in its shareholder letter that Bitcoin mining remains the company's core business. **[Image of image: https://img.jinse.com.cn/7524523]** **IV. Two-Way Failure: The Market Begins to Categorize Mining Companies** **The sharp fluctuations in the AI ​​sector in November disrupted this path.** According to a Bloomberg report on November 5th, Microsoft tightened its oversight of neocloud projects such as Nebius, IREN, and Nscale, withdrawing from projects it deemed risky and internally discussing whether to continue signing new neocloud contracts. On the same day, IREN, in its earnings report, postponed its annualized revenue target of over $4 billion from the end of 2026 to January 2027, stating that it might be delayed until February due to design changes requested by customers and supplier schedules. Subsequently, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 12th but was reinstated by the board on the 23rd. The stock price of the company, which had transitioned to mining, subsequently fluctuated wildly. Based on Nasdaq closing prices, from November 13th to 20th, IREN fell 34.9% in a week, MARA fell 27.2%, and Bitcoin fell approximately 15% during the same period. On the day Huang Renxun returned to office, mining stocks rebounded collectively, with IREN surging over 20%, before falling back 11.54% the following day. From the price trends, these companies' stock prices have increasingly followed AI sentiment, with Bitcoin taking a secondary role. A deeper problem lies in financing. The Bitcoin buffer has been sold, and most AI leases won't start until after 2027. During this period, construction funds can only rely on external financing. Unfortunately, the financing environment is tightening. IREN disclosed that approximately $6 billion in financing for the remaining capital expenditures in fiscal year 2027 remains unsecured, depending on market conditions. Cipher has agreed to assume the first $359.3 million over budget for the Barber Lake project. Riot management mentioned in the Q3 conference call that rising interest rates and widening credit spreads have led lenders to significantly tighten their scrutiny of tenants' credit, power supply, and delivery records. Project financing for the Corsicana project will not begin until 2027. If loans cannot be secured under market conditions, tenants will advance approximately $3.6 billion in construction costs, which will then be deducted from rent at an implied annual interest rate of approximately 12%. The market has also begun to reprice mining companies accordingly. As of the closing bell on November 24th, Riot was up 25.6% year-to-date, while IREN and Cipher were down 66.8% and 63.1% respectively, MARA was down 41.1%, TeraWulf was down 14.5%, and Bitcoin was down 31.5% year-to-date.

Riot, which has secured top tenants and doesn't currently need equity financing, is one of the few exceptions. IREN, which has purchased its own GPUs and still has a financing gap, saw the deepest decline.

Of course, based on publicly disclosed information, no signed leases have been cancelled yet. Mining companies are currently facing pressure from valuation, financing, and delivery.

V. Epilogue

Overall, it's difficult for mining companies to return to their original path. According to Hashrate Index estimates, the next halving will occur around April 2028, at which time the block reward will be halved again. CoinShares analyst Luke Nolan also believes that even if the price of Bitcoin recovers, it will be difficult to reverse the transformation of mining companies towards AI.

This also raises a bigger question. Listed mining companies were once the main force of Bitcoin's hash power; now that they are gradually transferring electricity and facilities to AI companies, who will take over the hash power they leave behind?

In May of this year, VanEck proposed that as US-listed mining companies shift their electricity to AI hyperscale customers, idle hydroelectric and natural gas resources controlled by governments will naturally succeed Bitcoin mining. If this assessment holds true, the security budget for the Bitcoin network will increasingly be borne by sovereign entities and low-cost energy providers, while Wall Street-backed listed mining companies will gradually become the electricity landlords of the AI ​​era. For Bitcoin, this may signify another shift in the computing power landscape, with a more decentralized and unpredictable group of participants taking over.
